1:
The book opens on a name the witnesses cannot agree to fix. The reformed John Gill surveys the field and clears away the easy candidates: this Ahasuerus cannot be the Astyages of Daniel 9:1, whose seat lay among the Medes and not at Shushan, nor the Cambyses whom many take for the Ahasuerus of Ezra 4:6, since by Ptolemy's canon Cambyses reigned but eight years where this king reigned at least twelve, and Cambyses was ever an enemy to the Jews, which this monarch was not. Gill weighs Bishop Usher's guess of Darius Hystaspis, a friend to the Jewish nation, yet the Midrash and many Jewish writers had made him the Artaxerxes of Ezra and Nehemiah, and toward that identification Gill himself inclines.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, following Lightfoot, takes him for the Artaxerxes who hindered the building of the temple, also called Ahasuerus in Ezra 4:6-7; and since Mordecai is said to have been carried captive from Jerusalem in Esther 2:5-6, Henry reasons that Ahasuerus must have been one of the earliest kings of that empire. Henry cares less for the man than for the moral of his greatness: such vast power in a bad hand can do the more mischief, and in a good hand the more good — and Christ's kingdom, he adds, shall one day be larger than this, and everlasting. The wesleyan-arminian voices pull apart. Adam Clarke, leaning on Prideaux, names him Artaxerxes Longimanus, the long-handed, who after bloody wars against the sons of Artabanus and his own brother Hystaspes settled the empire and, about his third year, some 462 years before Christ, began this history; Clarke sets the empire's bounds by Xenophon — the Red Sea to the east, the Euxine to the north, Cyprus and Egypt to the west, Ethiopia to the south. John Wesley, by contrast, supposes Darius Hystaspis, whose kingdom was thus vast, who subdued India as Herodotus reports, and one of whose wives, Atossa, differs little from Hadassah, Esther's other name in Esther 2:7.

Against them all the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott argues that of the three men called Ahasuerus in the Old Testament, this one is almost certainly Xerxes, who succeeded his father Darius Hystaspes in 485 before Christ and whose reign runs through Thermopylae and the rout at Salamis to his murder in 464. Keil and Delitzsch, opening their introduction, are content to summarize the argument — how the king feasted his grandees, divorced Vashti, and made way for the Jewess whose name the book bears. On the empire's reach the witnesses close ranks: it ran from India to Ethiopia over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, a number Henry and Wesley set beside the hundred and twenty princes of Daniel 6:1 — seven added, Wesley notes, to that older tally — while Ellicott traces how the Persian satrapies had swelled from twenty toward thirty, and holds that these provinces must take in their subdivisions. So overgrown a dominion, Henry warns, would in time sink under its own weight, losing its provinces as fast as it had gained them.
2:
The second verse takes up the date of the first and adds a new particular — the king "sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Shushan the palace" — and the witnesses part company over what that sitting signifies. The reformed John Gill reads it as settled repose: Ahasuerus was not merely placed on the throne but fixed and established there, having subdued Egypt in the second year of his reign and come into great peace and tranquillity. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that he was "settled in the peaceable possession" of his kingdom, and Adam Clarke likewise takes it of a king who, having subdued all his enemies, now enjoyed a universal quiet.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch expressly reject that reading. To "sit on the throne," they insist, does not carry the notion of quiet possession after the ending of wars — the sense Clericus and Rambach had pressed — but simply of being enthroned with royal authority. The Persian kings, they observe, are always represented upon a raised seat, even upon their journeys and in their battles: Xerxes, by Herodotus's account, watched the fight at Thermopylae sitting upon his throne, and Plutarch reports the same of him at Salamis. So the word marks not a lull in campaigning but the majesty of a reigning monarch, seated in state over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces.

On the setting the voices converge. Shushan, all agree, is Susa — Shuster, Clarke notes, to the later Persians — the ancient city that, with Ecbatana and Babylon, served the Persian kings for a residence; here, Wesley observes, they kept their winter court, retiring to Ecbatana in the summer heat. Clarke adds a point of translation: the Hebrew rendered "the palace" (habbirah) is better given as "the city," following the Septuagint, so that the citadel names the whole royal town. Keil and Delitzsch send the reader to the same fortress-city named in Nehemiah 1:1 and to Daniel's vision beside the Ulai at Susa in Daniel 8:2. The dispute, small as it looks, sets the book's tone: whether we are shown a conqueror resting from his wars or simply an absolute king enthroned in his winter capital, the throne itself is the fixed point from which every command in the chapter will proceed, and from which, in due time, the deliverance of a hidden people will be decreed as well. Keil observes that the very phrase "in those days" reaches back to take up the chronological note of the opening verse, binding the throne, the citadel, and the third-year feast into one connected scene; and the witnesses, for all their small quarrel over the sense of a single word, leave us the same picture in the end — the king not restless in the field but established in his hall, the whole weight of empire gathered into one seated figure whose lightest word is now become law.
3:
"In the third year of his reign he made a feast unto all his princes and his servants." The reformed John Gill confesses that the occasion cannot be fixed with certainty — whether the first day fell on the king's birthday, or on the anniversary of his accession, on which day, Herodotus relates, the Persian kings were accustomed to hold a yearly feast. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is bolder: assuming Ahasuerus to be Xerxes, the third year falls in 483 before Christ, precisely when Xerxes gathered his princes at Susa to arrange the invasion of Greece; a great banquet was the natural adjunct of so momentous a council, and rejoicing over the war lately concluded in Egypt might well have mingled with high hopes for the campaign to come.

Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar of the guest-list. "To make a feast" is the very idiom of Genesis 21:8; and the clause naming "the power of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces, being before him" is an independent circumstantial sentence, added to call attention to the vast number assembled at Susa — the chayil, or forces, which Bertheau would take of the royal body-guard rather than of an army in the field. Ellicott lingers over a single word: "nobles" renders the Persian partemim, literally "first," a term that recurs in Daniel 1:3 and Esther 6:9 and stands plainly akin to the Greek protos and the Latin primus.

So the witnesses give the verse two frames. To Gill it is a grand court festival whose pretext is uncertain but whose splendour is not; to Ellicott it is the opening scene of a war, the feasting of an empire's chieftains on the eve of the march that would end at Salamis. The two readings do not finally contradict — a king may celebrate a past victory, plan a coming one, and display his magnificence all in a single season — but they weight the feast differently, the one as royal ostentation, the other as the muster of a realm summoned to arms. What both agree upon is the scale: it was the whole strength of Persia and Media, its nobles and its provincial governors, that stood assembled before the throne, and no small company that the king was about to entertain. Gill adds that whatever the pretext, the season was one of open magnificence, the king ringed about with the flower of his realm; and Keil, following Bertheau, reads the very syntax as framed to fix our eyes upon the throng — the forces of Persia and Media all standing before their lord. Between the reformed reticence that will not name the day and the grammatical-historical confidence that dates it to the war-council of 483 before Christ, the verse keeps its double character, at once a festival kept in purple and the first muster of the host that Greece would one day break.
4:
The half-year of display draws the witnesses into open dispute. The verse says the king showed "the riches of his glorious kingdom and the honour of his excellent majesty" for a hundred and fourscore days, and the older reading, which the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley voices, takes this as one continuous festival — every day a magnificent feast, whether for all his princes together or for some coming successively, the Persian banquets being famed, as Wesley says, for their length and their luxury. Adam Clarke enlarges upon that luxury as the very badge of the Eastern monarchs, whose ostentation passed into a proverb, so that Horace could sneer, "Persicos odi, puer, apparatus" — I detest, boy, the grandeur of a Persian feast — and who drew from their poets and flatterers the highest encomiums for such shows.

The grammatical-historical witnesses will not have it that a banquet ran six months. Ellicott calls the notion, as a period of mere feasting, simply incredible, and insists the time must rather be understood as one during which troops were collected and the plan of invasion settled. Keil and Delitzsch press the same point from the text itself: it does not say the feast lasted a hundred and eighty days, and the common view rests on a misreading of the verse; the long span is the season of displaying the kingdom's wealth, the seven-day banquet of the next verse being the feast proper. Clericus had already softened the difficulty by supposing the grandees entertained in relays, since all could not be absent from their provinces for half a year; while Bertheau thought the historian meant only to excite astonishment, and that they who are astonished will not stop to ask how it was done.

The reformed John Gill turns the display toward prophecy. Xerxes, he notes, was the fourth and far the richest king of the Persian line, into whose hands all the treasure of his predecessors had flowed; and now began to be fulfilled the word that "by his strength, through his riches, he should stir up all against the realm of Grecia," the prophecy of Daniel 11:2. On this reading the parade of wealth was no idle vanity but the calculated summons of a king animating his nobles to the Grecian expedition, showing them the riches that should carry the war — which draws Gill's reformed sense of providence near to Ellicott's military reconstruction, both finding in the endless "feast" the mustering of an empire for its ruin. The dispute is not idle. On the literalists' reading the verse paints a half-year of unbroken revelry, a very debauch of wealth; on the historians' reading it paints a general staff at its work, the treasure spread out not for pleasure but for war. Either way the witnesses agree upon what is displayed — the whole substance of the empire, laid open to view, as though the king would keep back nothing of his glory from the eyes he had summoned to behold it.
5:
The great festival ends and a second, wider one begins. When the hundred and eighty days were expired, the reformed John Gill notes, in which the nobles and princes had been feasted, the king spread a table "unto all the people that were present in Shushan the palace, both unto great and small." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the descent: the first feast had been for the nobles at large, this for the people of the city without distinction; and because so numerous a company could be received in no apartment of the palace, the court of the garden was chosen to hold them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the gesture unremarkable for a Persian court, setting it beside Cyrus feasting "all the Persians" in Herodotus, while Keil and Delitzsch simply carry the narrative forward into the seven days in the garden court, some of the people coming on one day and some on another.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the whole extravagance and is not impressed. Two feasts Ahasuerus made, he observes — one for his nobles that ran its hundred and eighty days, and this for all the people; and he did not feast the same persons every day for all that time, but the nobles of one province perhaps on one day and another the next, while he and his constant attendants fared sumptuously throughout. The pride of his heart, rising with the grandeur of his kingdom, spent itself in vain glory, a pomp to no purpose, since none questioned his riches nor vied with him for honour. Had he laid out such wealth as some of his successors did, upon the building and the service of the temple, as those recorded in Ezra 7:22, it would have turned to a far better account. "Better," Henry sighs with the proverb of Proverbs 15:17, "is a dinner of herbs with quietness, and the enjoyment of one's self and a friend, than this banquet of wine with all the noise and tumult that must needs attend it." This history, he notes, comes in between the sixth and seventh chapters of Ezra; and the historians reconstruct its splendour while the moralist measures it, and finds a whole empire's magnificence lighter than a quiet meal. The witnesses divide their labour rather than their judgment: Clarke and Keil describe the garden thrown open because no hall could hold the multitude, Ellicott sets the open-handedness in its Persian frame, and Henry alone weighs the whole in the scale of eternity. Yet all of them feel the contrast the verse quietly draws, between the first feast for the great and this for the small — a king who could spend six months upon his nobles yet stoop to spread a table for the common people of Susa, so that even his condescension becomes a kind of display, and the humblest guest in the garden court is made one more witness to the honour of his majesty.
6:
The verse spreads before us the fabric and stonework of the garden court — its hangings "fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and pillars of marble" — and the witnesses turn philologists over its colours. The reformed John Gill reads "white, green, and blue hangings" as curtains of fine linen in those three hues, noting that the opening letter of the word for "white" is written larger than usual, to mark their exceeding whiteness; the second word, carpas, he takes, with Ben Melech, for a dyed colour said to be green, perhaps the Carpasian linen that Pausanias mentions, while the last denotes a sky-blue or hyacinth. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the rendering: the phrase should run "white cotton and blue," for carpas is not a colour but cotton, a word occurring only here in all the Hebrew, and white and blue, as Rawlinson remarks, were the royal colours of Persia.

Over the pavement the same divergence runs. The Authorized reading, which Gill follows, makes "red, and blue, and white, and black" so many colours of marble; Ellicott insists these are not colours at all but the names of actual stones, doubtful in meaning — bahat, which the Septuagint gives an emerald hue and which may be malachite; shesh, white marble; dar, a pearly stone; and sokhereth, black. He fixes "linen" too as white linen, the sense it bears in 2 Chronicles 5:12, and the "marble" of the pillars as white.

On the couches the voices agree. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains that such courts were commonly hung not only with curtains but with a canopy of rich stuffs slung on cords from side to side, and paved with coloured marbles or painted tiles — the very origin, he suggests, of the Mosaic work that the Greeks and Romans borrowed from the East; the "beds of gold and silver" he takes for couches covered with cloth of gold and silver, though Ellicott would refer the gold to the framework of the couch itself and not merely to its coverlets. John Wesley adds the homely reason such couches are named at all: in those eastern countries men did not sit at tables as we do, but reclined at meat upon beds. The reader is left to see a hall of white and violet and cotton, roofed with cloth of price and floored with figured stone, where the guests of the great king lay at ease on gold. The disagreement over carpas and the pavement-stones is more than antiquarian, for it measures how far the eye of the modern historian, armed with the cognate tongues, will correct the older versions that Gill still trusts. Yet neither reading dims the scene. Whether the court shone with green linen upon coloured marble or with white cotton upon named and precious stones, the witnesses leave us the same impression of a wealth poured out upon mere furniture — the very floor and hangings of a week's feast worth the ransom of a province.
7:
"They gave them drink in vessels of gold, the vessels being diverse one from another." The reformed John Gill fastens on that diversity: the cups, though all of gold, differed in pattern and in workmanship, and the very variety made the festival the more magnificent. Among the Persians, he adds, earthen cups were counted mean — a king would disgrace a man by condemning him to drink from earthenware — so that a table of gold, no two pieces alike, was itself a proclamation of royal wealth. Gill then turns aside to correct a Jewish tradition: the Targum makes these the golden vessels of the temple that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off, but that cannot be, for those had already been delivered by Cyrus into the hand of Zerubbabel, as Ezra 1:7-11 records; they were long since back in Jerusalem, and not to be found upon a Persian sideboard.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the words. Keil and Delitzsch hear an exclamation in the Hebrew — "drinks poured into vessels of gold! and vessels differing from vessels, and royal wine in abundance, according to the hand of a king" — the piling of clauses meant to convey the sheer profusion. Charles Ellicott draws the larger inference: that the whole population of Susa could be thus accommodated in gold shows the immense treasures in the hand of the Persian king. The "royal wine" he thinks may be the celebrated wine of Helbon named in Ezekiel 27:18, for the original seems to promise more than merely wine from the royal cellars — and since the king was feasting his own people, it could scarcely have been otherwise; the closing phrase "according to the state of the king" is, he notes, literally "according to the hand of a king," the measure of a monarch's open-handedness. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says only, and plainly, that the guests were served from different services of plate. The witnesses do not quarrel here. They agree that the gold and the wine alike are set down to one purpose, the display of a wealth so vast that a whole city could be feasted from the royal treasury and never exhaust it. Gill's little excursus on the temple vessels is worth its space, for it quietly guards the honour of the sanctuary: the holy cups were not among these, having been restored to Jerusalem, and the Persian gold upon the tables of Susa was the king's own and no plunder of the house of God. The point turns the verse, for a moment, back toward the covenant people whose deliverance the book will tell; even here, amid the pomp of a heathen court, the witnesses will not let the vessels of the Lord be confounded with the vessels of Ahasuerus.
8:
"And the drinking was according to the law; none did compel." The verse turns on that restraint, and the witnesses gather to praise it. The reformed John Gill explains the rule the king laid on his officers: no man was to be obliged to drink beyond his own choice; the Targum glosses it "according to the custom of his body," that is, as each was able to bear. Gill sets the mercy against the degeneracy of the age — the old Persian temperance had given way, Xenophon complains, to such excess that the drinkers had at last to be carried out, unable to walk upright — and against the Greek rule of the feast, "drink or begone," which Ahasuerus here forbade, and against the master who ordered that Empedocles must drink or have the wine poured upon his head.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke heaps up the parallels the king's law overturns: the Greek proverb that a guest must keep the round or leave, the Roman arbiter bibendi chosen by the cast of the dice to prescribe the drinking to all the company, and George Herbert's stern verses in "The Church Porch" against the tyranny of the health that is sent round. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a nicety of sense: "law" here is rather an ordinance or decree issued specially for this occasion, by which the king ordered that all should do as they pleased in the matter of drinking, instead of being pressed, as usual, to drink — the more remarkable, he says, because the Persians had once been a nation of exceptionally temperate habits. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the plain meaning, that the king had appointed the officers of his house to serve every man according to his own pleasure.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and Wesley draw the moral home. There was here no forcing of healths, Henry observes, no sending the glass about; every man drank as he would, so that any excess was his own fault — a fault few would commit when the king's own order had put an honour upon sobriety. And this caution of a heathen prince, he says, may shame the many, called Christians, who think they cannot make their friends welcome unless they make them drunk, and who, under pretence of sending the health round, send the sin round, and death with it. Let them read the woe of Habakkuk 2:15-16, Henry urges, and tremble; for to rob a man of his reason, his richest jewel, is the greatest wrong that can be done him. So the witnesses turn a single clause into a small mirror for their own times. Gill and Ellicott fix the history, that a once-temperate people had learned to drink to ruin and that the king's order ran against the grain of the age; Clarke ransacks Greece and Rome for the very compulsions it forbade; and Henry and Wesley hold the heathen decree up as a rebuke to Christian tables, where the sin is too often pressed upon a guest as a courtesy. The verse commends a pagan king for a restraint that many who name Christ have not learned.
9:
While the king feasts the men, "Vashti the queen made a feast for the women in the royal house." The reformed John Gill explains the separate table by custom: it was not the way of the Persians, nor of the other eastern nations, to admit women to their festivals, so the queen kept hers apart. Who Vashti was he cannot certainly say — Usher takes her for Atossa, the daughter of Cyrus; the Targum makes her the daughter of Evilmerodach, Nebuchadnezzar's son; her name he thinks Persian, akin to Vesta, the fire the Persians venerated, and signifying vehement flame. The wesleyan-arminian voices agree on the custom: Adam Clarke reads the name as a Persian word for a beautiful or excellent woman and notes that the women of the East never mingle with the men in public, so that Vashti entertained the Persian ladies while the men sat in the garden court; John Wesley says the same, that men and women did not feast together.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott opens the harder question of her history. One wife among the Persians, he explains, was supreme over the rest, as Atossa the mother of Xerxes had been, and such, before her fall, was Vashti; yet the Greek writers name the queen of Xerxes not Vashti but Amestris, a woman of notorious cruelty, whom Herodotus makes the cousin of Xerxes, the daughter of his father's brother. Some would identify the two, Rawlinson supposing Vashti and Amestris to be different renderings of one Persian name and the deposition only a temporary one, while Bishop Wordsworth would rather make Amestris a wife of great influence between Vashti's fall and Esther's rise; Ellicott himself doubts the whole identification, and firmly refuses to make Esther one with the dissolute Amestris. He notes too that the Hebrew wants the article — not "the women," but simply "women."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry looks past the genealogy to the propriety. While the king made a show of the honour of his majesty, Vashti and her ladies, feasting privately in the royal house and not openly in the court of the garden, showed the honour of their modesty — which, Henry says, is truly the majesty of the fair sex. The witnesses thus leave Vashti half in shadow: a queen of uncertain lineage and disputed name, whose one recorded act before her ruin is a becoming reserve. The disputed genealogy matters less than the pattern the witnesses jointly draw. Whether Vashti was Cyrus's granddaughter, or Nebuchadnezzar's, or the cruel Amestris under another name, all agree that she was a great queen keeping a great queen's separate state, and that the propriety of her women's feast will presently be set over against the impropriety of the summons that breaks it. The reserve Henry praises in this verse is the very reserve the next verse will punish; and so the quiet notice of a separate banquet is laid down, deliberately, as the ground on which the whole quarrel is about to be fought.
10:
"On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine," the feast turns toward its ruin. The reformed John Gill notes that this seventh and last day was, by Jarchi and the Targum, the sabbath. Keil and Delitzsch read the king's temper plainly — the wine had made him merry — and it was in that state that he summoned his seven chamberlains to fetch the queen with the royal crown, to show her beauty to the people and the princes. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms from the eighth verse how freely the Persians indulged in wine, renders "chamberlains" more exactly "eunuchs," and observes that the very listing of all seven strange names — apparently not even Persian — betrays a writer of personal knowledge; Adam Clarke adds that these names, disguised in passing through the Hebrew, are Persian still, Mehuman signifying a stranger or a guest.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the merry verse into a lament. Here is a damp to all the mirth of the feast, he says, which ended in heaviness — not, like Job's children's feast, by a wind from the wilderness, nor, like Belshazzar's, by a hand-writing on the wall, but by the king's own folly. It was his weakness to send for Vashti while he was drunk and his guests with him; in commanding her to be shown he dishonoured himself as a husband, who ought to protect and by no means expose the modesty of his wife — she should have been to him "a covering of the eyes," in the phrase of Genesis 20:16, and not uncovered before a hall of revellers. And he diminished himself as a king, in demanding of his wife a thing she might honourably refuse, against the very custom of the Persians. Had he not been put out of possession of himself by drink, Henry judges, he would have been angry at any man who so much as proposed it; but when the wine is in, the wit is out, and a man's reason departs from him. The scene is set for the collision: an intoxicated monarch, seven eunuchs dispatched, and a crown carried toward a queen who will not wear it on such terms. The witnesses divide the scene between them without dividing over it. The historians fix the drunken hour, the eunuchs, and the crown; the reformed voice marks the sabbath; and Henry supplies the conscience, reading the summons as a double self-injury by which the king wounded at once his honour as a husband and his dignity as a king. What none of them misses is the pivot the verse turns upon: up to the seventh day all has been splendour, and now, with three words — merry with wine — the splendour begins to curdle, and the command that goes out with the crown becomes the first act of a folly that will cost the king his queen, and open, though he cannot know it, a place at his side for another.
11:
The command itself — "to bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people and the princes her beauty" — draws the witnesses to weigh its decency. The reformed John Gill puts the innocent construction first: it was not that the king would drag her by force, but that his chamberlains were to signify his pleasure that she come to him, and come at once. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the darker Jewish tradition preserved in the Targum, that she was to be brought naked, wearing the crown and nothing beside; and he ties her very name, Vashti, "beautiful," to the clause "for she was fair to look on" — so that the beauty which had first won her the throne was now to be paraded before a drunken hall, the modest queen of Esther 1:9 summoned to become a spectacle.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the king's demand as self-evidently the product of drink: it is plain from the very way the incident is introduced that a sober Ahasuerus would never have asked such a thing, and that Vashti, as any modest woman must, naturally sends back a refusal. On the "crown royal" he pauses to describe the object — a tall cap decked with gems and bound with a linen fillet of blue and white, this fillet being properly the diadem, as Trench distinguishes the two words. The witnesses do not divide over the fact, only over how much to say of it: Gill softens the command to a bare summons, Clarke and Ellicott let its indecency stand plain. What they share is the sense that the crown, meant to adorn the queen for a drunken exhibition, is about to become the emblem of the king's own shame; for the beauty he would display before his princes she will refuse to bring, and the diadem he sends will presently be given to another. The order that opens so grandly, with a queen fetched in her crown, is already bending toward the humiliation of the very throne that issued it. There is a deeper irony the witnesses feel without quite naming it. The king would set his wife's beauty on show as the crown of all his other riches, the last and fairest item in a half-year's inventory of glory; but a queen is not a hanging or a golden cup, to be fetched out and displayed at a drunkard's whim, and in the very act of trying to exhibit her he loses her. Gill's gentler reading and Ellicott's blunter one meet in this, that the demand was the king's alone and the shame that follows his own; and Vashti's refusal, when it comes, will only hold up before him the mirror of his folly.
12:
"But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment." The refusal is the hinge of the chapter, and the witnesses divide over how to judge it. The reformed John Gill defends her motives: though the king sent again, as the Targum and Josephus say, she would not come — not from pride or contempt, but because she judged him drunk, and knew that were he sober he might blame her, or worse, for having appeared; besides, it was against the law of the Persians, as Josephus and Plutarch both note, for wives to be seen in public, so that to be summoned thus was to be treated as a harlot or a concubine, an indignity she would not bear. Keil and Delitzsch read her the same way — she would not stake her dignity as queen and wife before his inebriated guests, knowing the audacity of Persians in that condition — and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the very law of Persia, keeping wives and above all queens from other men's view, favoured her refusal.

Adam Clarke turns defence into open praise. What woman of common prudence and modesty, he asks, could consent to expose herself before a group of drunken Bacchanalians? Her courage was equal to her modesty; she would resist the royal mandate rather than violate chaste decorum, though she well knew it might cost her the crown, if not her life. "Hail, noble woman!" he cries; be thou a pattern to all thy sex — a black swan, a bird rarely seen on earth.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry alone hesitates. Perhaps, he allows, it was not her wisdom to deny him; the thing commanded was not in itself sinful, and had she come in plain obedience it would have been no reflection on her modesty but rather her honour to comply. Yet if she refused in a haughty manner, scorning to come at the king's word, then her refusal was certainly evil. What a mortification, Henry adds, that while the king was showing the glory of his kingdom he should show the reproach of his own family, having a wife that would do as she pleased. Either way he finds the deeper folly on the throne: the king thereupon grew outrageous, and he that ruled a hundred and twenty-seven provinces had no rule over his own spirit, but let his anger burn in him. So the witnesses leave a real division — most crown Vashti's refusal as modest courage; Henry, alone, will not pronounce it wise until he knows the spirit in which it was made. Yet even Henry's caution bends, in the end, toward the throne's greater fault: whatever spirit moved the queen, it was the king who turned a private slight into a public rage, and a wiser man, he grants, would have stifled the affront and turned it off with a jest rather than blaze it abroad before his princes. The witnesses thus leave Vashti admired and the king pitied — a queen whose worst fault may have been a proud tone, a monarch whose folly has now armed the whole apparatus of the state against his own household.
13:
The angry king turns for counsel "to the wise men, which knew the times," and the witnesses cannot agree who these men were. The reformed John Gill offers two guesses at once: astrologers, as Aben Ezra thought, who knew the fit and fortunate time for any undertaking; or else men learned in history, versed in the records of former ages, who could match the present case to some precedent. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch come down for the first: those "who knew the times" are astrologers and magi, who give their counsel according to the phenomena of the heavens, like the wise men of Babylon summoned in Daniel 2:27 and again in Daniel 5:15, and the astrologers and stargazers of Isaiah 47:13.

The other grammatical-historical witness pulls the opposite way. Charles Ellicott takes them for men skilled in precedents, who could advise the king from what had been done before; and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees, guessing them "probably the lawyers." John Wesley leans toward history: "the times," he says, are the histories of former ages, and the wise men those who knew what princes had done in cases such as this. So the counsellors are variously cast — diviners reading the stars, jurists reading the statute-book, historians reading the annals — and the witnesses will not settle which craft the verse intends.

Keil and Delitzsch add the sense of the parenthesis that follows: "for so was the king's manner toward all that knew law and judgment." The word our version renders "matter," they observe, means not speech but business; and the clause tells us that in every affair the king, before deciding, laid the case before those skilled in law and judgment to hear their opinion. Ellicott renders it to the same effect, "for so was the king's business laid before" his advisers. Whatever the wise men's precise office — and it is left in doubt — all the voices agree on the habit the verse reveals: this absolute monarch, who could not govern his own temper, would not so much as sentence his own queen except by the forms of law and the counsel of his princes. The threefold guess is itself instructive, for it shows how little the verse yields to certainty and how much each school brings to it. The grammatical-historical Keil hears the language of Babylon's stargazers and reads magi; the same school's Ellicott, and the wesleyan Clarke, hear the language of the courts and read jurists; Wesley, and Gill in his second mind, hear the language of the chronicles and read historians. What unites them is larger than what divides: a king in a passion, who might have spoken one word and had his queen dragged before him or put away, instead pauses to summon the wisest heads in his realm — whether they read the stars, the statutes, or the annals — and will not stir until they have spoken.
14:
The seven counsellors are named — "Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan" — and the witnesses fill in their rank. The reformed John Gill takes "the next unto him" for the man who sat nearest the king, first in dignity and in authority under him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls the seven the king's privy counsellors, and reads "which saw the king's face" as the mark of men admitted at all times to the royal presence. John Wesley enlarges the point: to see the king's face meant a constant freedom of access and a familiar converse with him, the more notable because the Persian kings were very seldom seen by their subjects, but kept themselves withdrawn in a jealous seclusion; and "sat the first in the kingdom" marks these seven his chief officers and counsellors of state.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the seven in their constitutional place. They are the heads of the seven leading families of Persia, the king's standing advisers, the same body as the "seven counsellors" of Ezra 7:14 by whom Artaxerxes sent Ezra to Jerusalem, and the seven nobles of whom Herodotus tells, who rose against the false Smerdis and set Darius on the throne. Ellicott ventures even to recognize history in two of the names — Marsena may be the Mardonius who commanded at Marathon, and Admatha the Artabanus who was uncle to Xerxes. Keil and Delitzsch note only what the next verses will need: that Memucan, though named last in the roll, will presently come forward as the spokesman of them all.

So the verse, a bare list of seven names, opens into a glimpse of the Persian constitution. Here is a great king who cannot be approached at will, seldom seen even by his own people, yet girt about by seven hereditary princes who alone look upon his face and sit first in his kingdom; and it is to these — not to any court of law, nor to the queen's own kindred — that he now brings his domestic quarrel. The witnesses agree in painting the scene: an empire's whole machinery of counsel, its oldest and greatest houses, convened at a drunken feast to decide what shall be done with a wife who would not come when she was called. The witnesses, gathering these details, let the pathos and the peril of the moment show through the dry list. Wesley's seldom-seen king, walled about with ceremony; Clarke's privy council of the seven; Ellicott's hereditary houses that had once made and unmade kings — all of it converges upon a single small question of domestic order, as though the constitution of an empire had been convened to try a quarrel over a banquet. And Keil's quiet note, that the last-named of the seven will be the one to speak, warns the reader where the weight will fall: the gravest counsel will come from the least of the counsellors, and a whole realm's law will be shaped by the youngest voice at the table.
15:
The king's question — "What shall we do unto the queen Vashti according to law, because she hath not performed the commandment of the king Ahasuerus by the chamberlains?" — is brief, and the witnesses here are few. The reformed John Gill reads it simply: the king desired to know what law was provided for such a case, and what, according to that law, should be done to her. Keil and Delitzsch set it in the same key — the monarch, greatly incensed at this defiance of his behest, inquires of his wise men what is to be done to the queen according to law, and not what his own anger might dictate.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out what the question quietly concedes. Two things he bids us observe: that though it was the queen who was guilty, the law must nonetheless have its course; and that though the king was very angry, he would yet do nothing but what he was advised was according to law. There is, in this, an unexpected restraint — passion made to wait upon precedent, and even an absolute will submitting its private quarrel to the forms of public justice. Henry finds in it, too, a lesson on counsel: the greater a man's power, he says, the greater his need of advice, that he may not abuse that power; and of such counsellors, in the proverb of Proverbs 11:14, in their multitude there is safety.

So the smallest verse of the debate carries its own irony. A king who a moment before had no rule over his own spirit now insists that everything be done by rule; the man who could not command his temper will not command even his queen except "according to law." The witnesses leave the question hanging where the narrative itself leaves it, upon the threshold of the counsellor's answer — with the whole weight of the empire's law about to descend upon a domestic quarrel born at a banquet, and a private slight about to be dressed in the robes of a public cause. It is the hinge on which Vashti's crown will turn. The reformed Gill and the grammatical-historical Keil are content to state the question; it is the puritan Henry who hears in it the deeper note, that a king enslaved to his own anger is yet the servant of his own laws, and must let precedent decide what passion would have settled in a moment. There is warning in it, and there is mercy too: warning, that the forms of law, once invoked, will grind on past the point where the angry man might have relented; mercy, that even a heathen court will not let a queen be ruined by a mere fit of temper, but must first ask what the law provides.
16:
Memucan rises to answer, and the witnesses weigh both his standing and his logic. The reformed John Gill notes that Memucan, named last of the seven, was perhaps the least and the youngest, and that by the king's own appointment — so the later Targum has it — the least of the counsellors was to give his opinion first, much as with us the puisne judges and the youngest peers deliver their judgment before the elder. Keil and Delitzsch report the substance of his verdict: speaking for all after their joint consultation, he declared before the king and the princes, in solemn assembly, that Vashti had wronged not the king alone but all the princes and all the people, since her example would teach every wife in Persia and Media to despise her husband; and therefore an irrevocable edict must go forth against her.

Over the soundness of that reasoning the witnesses divide sharply. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls it inconsequent and false: Vashti had not disobeyed generally but in this one particular only, and so could be no precedent for the conduct of Persian women at large; Memucan drew a single act into a sweeping consequence, and the rest assented, being either too drunk to tell right from wrong, or too intent on reducing their wives to a settled vassalage to let so fair an occasion slip. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads him as a practised courtier, who gives his master exactly the palatable advice that echoes the king's own angry question; the phrase "done wrong," he adds, is more literally "dealt unfairly."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry is more willing to grant Memucan a good motive. Some suppose, he allows, that the counsellor gave this severe advice only because he knew it would please the king and gratify his passion; but Josephus says, on the contrary, that the king had a strong affection for Vashti, and would not have put her away for this offence had the law let him pass it by — in which case we must credit Memucan with a sincere regard for justice and for the public good. So the witnesses leave the counsellor's word doubly lit: to Clarke and Ellicott a piece of drunken flattery dressed up as statecraft, to Henry a possibly honest fear that private disorder, once made public, would unsettle every household in the realm. The division is a real one, and the witnesses do not paper it over. To the wesleyan and grammatical-historical readers Memucan is a flatterer, magnifying a private slight into a public peril to please a drunken master and to tighten every husband's grip; to the puritan he may be an honest statesman, seeing further than the king himself and fearing, not without reason, that disorder at the throne will breed disorder in every home. What all of them agree upon is the disproportion the verse enshrines — that one woman's refusal at one banquet is now solemnly pronounced a wrong done to all the princes and all the peoples of a hundred and twenty-seven provinces.
17:
Memucan presses his alarm into the future: "this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto all women, so that they shall despise their husbands in their eyes." The reformed John Gill hears in it the speed of rumour — the thing will soon be spread through all the king's dominions, reach the ears of every wife, and become the common talk everywhere. Keil and Delitzsch simply carry the argument on toward the proposal it is framed to justify, the counsellor building his case for a decree upon the certainty that the queen's refusal cannot be kept hidden.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the reasoning that the bare verse compresses. Had the quarrel between the king and queen remained private, Henry says, the error would have stayed with themselves and might have been quietly settled; but being public — and the very ladies then feasting with Vashti perhaps well pleased at her refusal — her example was likely to work upon all the families of the kingdom. If the queen might have her humour and the king must submit, then, since the houses of private persons commonly take their measures from the courts of princes, wives everywhere would grow haughty and imperious and scorn to obey, and the poor despised husbands might fret at it but could not help themselves. The contentions of such a wife, Henry recalls, are "a continual dropping," in the words of Proverbs 19:13 and again of Proverbs 27:15; and where wives despise the husbands they ought to reverence, as Ephesians 5:33 enjoins, and contend for dominion over those to whom 1 Peter 3:1 bids them be in subjection, there cannot but follow continual guilt and grief. The witnesses agree in substance: the counsellor's fear, whether shrewd or self-serving, is that one queen's refusal at Shushan will echo as a thousand refusals in every province of the empire. Henry lets the argument run to its end and finds it, for all its self-interest, not wholly false: where the reverence a wife owes is exchanged for contempt, and the subjection she is called to for a struggle after mastery, there follows in truth continual guilt and grief, and the peace of a house is worn through by a proud spirit as a roof is worn through by a ceaseless dropping. Yet the witnesses let the reader see the exaggeration too. Memucan speaks as though a single act at court would topple the order of every household from Ethiopia to India; and there is something at once shrewd and comic in a council of half-drunken statesmen persuading themselves that the safety of marriage throughout the world hangs upon the humbling of one queen. The verse stands, then, as both a real word about the honour due within a home and a wry exposure of the panic of powerful men.
18:
"Likewise shall the ladies of Persia and Media say this day unto all the king's princes." The counsellor turns from wives at large to the great ladies of the court, and the reformed John Gill reads the threat as immediate: from this very day the princesses, having heard of the queen's deed, will give their own husbands the like answer, telling them to their faces that they will not obey. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the word — the Hebrew saroth means the princesses, though "ladies" renders it well enough — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the translation: "this day," he would render, "shall the princesses of Persia and Media, which heard the affair of the queen, say" the same to all the king's princes. The closing phrase, "thus shall there arise too much contempt and wrath," Ellicott resolves into its two halves — contemptuous defiance on the part of the wives, and answering anger on the part of the husbands; John Wesley reads it exactly so, contempt in the wives and wrath in the husbands, and consequently strife in families throughout the land.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a picture of domestic ruin. When wives despise the husbands whom they ought to reverence, and contend for the dominion they were never given, there follows, he says, continual guilt and grief, confusion and every evil work — the very disorder that James 3:16 lays at the door of envying and strife; and therefore, he warns, the great must take special heed of the copies they set, since the households of a whole kingdom will pattern themselves upon its court. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Memucan's argument has now reached its sharpest point: the queen's single refusal is made to threaten not merely disorder in this or that home, but a general insurrection of wives against husbands throughout the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, and the peace of the empire itself is pleaded as bound up with the obedience of its women. The grammatical-historical witnesses give the verse its sharper edges — Clarke recovering the princesses beneath the pale word "ladies," Ellicott mending the tense so that the threat lands "this day," and both, with Wesley, parsing the closing phrase into its twin passions of a wife's contempt and a husband's wrath. Henry supplies the end of the road they are on: contempt breeding wrath, wrath breeding strife, and strife breeding that confusion and every evil work in which a household, like a kingdom, comes undone. The witnesses do not so much argue as accumulate, each adding a stroke to the same portrait — a court frightened by its own queen into imagining a whole empire of rebellious wives, and reaching, for so domestic a fear, after the heaviest instrument it owns.
19:
Memucan comes at last to his remedy: "let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered." The reformed John Gill marks the weight of it — not a mere proclamation but a law formally enacted and published by royal authority. Keil and Delitzsch render the proposal's opening as "let there go from him a word of the kingdom," that is, a royal edict; and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains the fatal clause "that it be not altered": the decree was to be inserted among the permanent laws, made part of the very constitution of the empire, so that — the Persians affecting such wisdom in their legislation that their laws should never be amended nor repealed — men could speak proverbially of the laws of the Medes and Persians that change not.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same phrase more literally as "that it pass not away," the order once committed to writing being, in theory at least, immutable; the best illustration, he says, is the well-known case of Daniel and the decree that even a grieving king could not revoke in Daniel 6:8, and the like inviolability meets us again in Esther 8:8 — though he dryly adds that a strong-willed monarch would learn to interpret such inviolability freely enough. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry attends to the sentence pronounced: the judgment that Vashti "come no more before king Ahasuerus," her royal estate given to another better than she, and the whole so ratified as never to be reversed.

The witnesses do not contend. They agree that a domestic slight has been turned, in a single stroke of counsel, into an unrepealable law of the realm — that Vashti's crown is forfeit past recall. And there is an irony the reader is meant to feel: this same machinery of Medo-Persian law, which here shuts fast upon a disobedient queen, will one day shut fast upon the king himself, when his own irrevocable decree against the Jews cannot be recalled but only outrun. The rigidity that ruins Vashti is the very rigidity through which, in the end, a hidden providence will work the deliverance of a people. On the plain matter the witnesses are agreed: Gill's formal enactment, Keil's "word of the kingdom," Clarke's and Ellicott's unrepealable statute, and Henry's sentence of perpetual banishment all describe one thing — a queen cast down for ever by a law that cannot be recalled. What gives the verse its force is the machinery it introduces, the boast of a legislation too wise ever to be changed; and the reader who knows the book smiles grimly, for that very boast will return to torment the throne, when a decree procured by Haman can no more be revoked than this one, and the king who so lightly unmakes a queen will find he cannot so lightly unmake a sentence of death.
20:
"And when the king's decree which he shall make shall be published throughout all his empire (for it is great), all the wives shall give to their husbands honour, both to great and small." The reformed John Gill notes only how fit it was that the decree be proclaimed everywhere, since the report of the queen's own deed would travel just as far, and the remedy must reach as wide as the offence. Keil and Delitzsch carry the sense forward: the edict, published through so great an empire, was to secure that every wife, of high station and low alike, should render honour to her husband — and to that end letters would be sent into every province "according to its writing, and to every people according to their speech," as again in Esther 8:9, that the king's will might be plainly understood by subjects of many tongues and scripts.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the design of it. The hoped consequence, he says, was that wives would give their husbands honour — the wives of the great notwithstanding their own greatness, and the wives of the small notwithstanding their husbands' meanness — so that every man might bear rule in his own house as he ought, and, the wife being subject, the children and the servants would fall into order too. For it is the interest of states and kingdoms, Henry observes, to provide that good order be kept in private families, the household being the commonwealth in little, and public peace built up out of a thousand quiet homes.

The witnesses agree upon the aim while quietly exposing its overreach. An empire that has just watched its own king lose all rule over himself now legislates that every husband shall rule his home; a court whose one recorded marriage has ended in public rupture publishes in every language of the realm a decree meant to mend by statute the very reverence that no statute can command. The honour of wives cannot be enacted like a tax; and the reader, who knows already what a hidden hand is doing behind these edicts, sees the great machine of Persian law grinding out a rule about domestic order while it unknowingly clears the way for a new queen. Gill and Keil describe the decree's reach, Henry its domestic aim, and the reader supplies the irony none of them can miss: that a court should try to secure by proclamation the one thing a proclamation cannot reach. Honour freely given is honour; honour commanded is only fear, and the very need to legislate it confesses that it has already failed at the top. Yet the witnesses close on a graver note than satire, for it is by just such follies that the unnamed God of this book is pleased to work, and the same courier who carries a law about the ruling of husbands carries, all unknowing, the first stroke of a providence that will set a Jewish orphan upon the throne of Persia.
21:
"And the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan." The reformed John Gill reads the assent as unanimous — the king and the other six princes and counsellors all approved the proposal and agreed together to it. Keil and Delitzsch add that the king at once carried it into execution, sending letters into all his provinces to make his will known and to teach every husband that he was to bear rule in his own house.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the verse into providence, and here the chapter's hidden theme breaks the surface. Whether it was the king's passion or his policy that was served by this decree, Henry says, God's providence served its own purpose by it — which was to make way for Esther to the crown. The book will nowhere name God, yet Henry sees his finger in these minute events: the drunken quarrel, the counsellor's advice, the irrevocable edict, all conspiring, unknown to the very men who made them, to depose the queen whose place a daughter of the captives would fill, so that Haman's murderous project should be defeated even before it had entered his heart or he had climbed to his power. The elevation of Esther, told in Esther 2:17, has its true beginning here, in a decree aimed at nothing higher than the honour of husbands.

Let us rejoice, Henry urges, that the Lord reigns, and will overrule the madness and the folly of mankind to promote his own glory and the safety and happiness of his people. The witnesses leave the verse as a quiet turning-point, and it is the more eloquent for its quietness: a king thinks he is merely disciplining his wife; his princes think they are merely securing their own homes; and heaven, working through their wine and their wrath and their small statecraft, is opening the one door through which, years hence, an entire people will be drawn back from the edge of destruction. Gill's unanimous council and Keil's swift execution give the fact; Henry gives the meaning, and it is the meaning the whole chapter has been bending toward. The book of Esther will name no miracle and record no prayer answered from heaven, yet here, at its first turning, the witnesses teach the reader how to read it: not as a court intrigue that happened to spare the Jews, but as a history in which every drunken word and proud refusal and flattering counsel is being woven, by a hand that never appears, into the rescue of a threatened people. The throne that Vashti loses in a night's folly is being kept, though none at Susa knows it, for the woman through whom deliverance will come.
22:
The chapter closes with the decree gone out: "he sent letters into all the king's provinces, into every province according to the writing thereof, and to every people after their language." The reformed John Gill notes that the letters went to all the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, written and sealed, as the Targum has it, with the king's own seal, that none might doubt their authority. Keil and Delitzsch, and the plain sense with them, take the verse to mean that the edict was sent to each province in its own script and to each people in its own tongue, as again in Esther 8:9, so that so vast and various an empire might all understand it alike.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott pauses over both the machinery and the words. The Persian Empire, he observes, was the first to possess a regular postal system, by which such letters could fly to the ends of the realm; and the Greek word for "compel" in Matthew 5:41 is itself, he notes, a corruption of the Persian term for the impressment of men and horses into the royal courier-service. But over the decree's last clause he parts from the common reading. Literally, he says, the Hebrew runs "that every man should be ruling in his own house, and speaking according to the language of his own people" — the first half betraying how much undue female influence there must already have been in Persia, the second meaning that in a household of foreign wives the husband must see to it that his own tongue is not supplanted by theirs; the Authorized Version, which makes the clause merely repeat that the decree was published in every language, does, he thinks, distinct violence to the Hebrew.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is frankly unimpressed with the whole enactment. That a man should bear rule in his own house was taught, he says, by God's law and by common sense from the very foundation of the world; the decree therefore established nothing new, and the whole parade of legislation was made, he suspects, only to strip honest Vashti of her crown. The Targum's addition, that each woman should also speak her husband's language, he leaves standing as unproven. So the book's first chapter ends upon a note of irony the witnesses do not miss: a king who could not rule himself sends his couriers racing to the ends of the earth to command that every other man shall rule his own house. Beneath the irony the witnesses leave a serious point. Gill's sealed letters, Keil's many scripts and tongues, Ellicott's imperial post and disputed clause, and Clarke's shrug at a law that changed nothing all describe the same vast apparatus of Persian rule — swift, literate, and absolute — now set in motion over the smallest of matters. It is that apparatus, so easily moved to fence in a queen and lecture a continent of husbands, that the reader is meant to mark; for the same couriers and the same unbreakable decrees will soon carry a sentence of death against a whole people, and the deliverance, when it comes, must come through the very machine that here grinds so grandly for so little.
